facts.statement: Austriadraco lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Norian stage between 217 and 213 million years ago, in present-day Austria.
facts.quote: Austriadraco is a genus of pterosaur living during the Late Triassic (Norian stage, 217-213 million years ago) in the area of present Austria.

facts.statement: Bernd Lammerer discovered the Austriadraco skeleton in June 1994 on a mountain trail near Seefeld in Austrian Tirol at an altitude of 1600 metres.
facts.quote: In June 1994, near Seefeld in Austrian Tirol, at a 1600 metres high mountain trail to the Reither Spitze, in the vicinity of the Reither Joch-Alm, Bernd Lammerer discovered a pterosaur skeleton.

facts.statement: The fossil remains of Austriadraco were recovered as five stone plates that were removed multiple times.
facts.quote: The remains have been secured as five stone plates, removed on several occasions.

facts.statement: In 2003, Peter Wellnhofer initially identified the fossil as a specimen of Eudimorphodon ranzii.
facts.quote: In 2003, Peter Wellnhofer identified the fossil as a specimen of Eudimorphodon, a cf. E. ranzii.

facts.statement: Peter Wellnhofer considered the specimen a juvenile because it was 10 to 25% shorter than the holotype of Eudimorphodon.
facts.quote: As it was 10 to 25% shorter than the latter's holotype, Wellnhofer considered it a juvenile.

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner named the genus Austriadraco in 2015, designating Austriadraco dallavecchiai as the type species.
facts.quote: In 2015, Alexander Kellner named the separate genus Austriadraco, with the type species Austriadraco dallavecchiai.

facts.statement: The generic name Austriadraco combines the Latin words for Austria and dragon.
facts.quote: The generic name is a combination of the Latin words Austria and draco, "dragon".

facts.statement: The specific name dallavecchiai honors Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia.
facts.quote: The specific name honours Dalla Vecchia.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen BSP 1994 I 51 was found in the Seefeld Formation dating from the late Norian.
facts.quote: The holotype, BSP 1994 I 51, was found in a layer of the Seefeld Formation, dating from the late Norian.

facts.statement: The holotype consists of a partial and disarticulated skeleton that includes a skull.
facts.quote: It consists of a partial and disarticulated skeleton with skull.

facts.statement: The skeleton includes frontal bones, a left jugal, lower jaws, loose teeth, vertebrae from the neck to the tail, the shoulder girdle, humeri, a wing phalanx, the pelvis, and leg bones.
facts.quote: It contains both frontal bones, a left jugal, the lower jaws, loose teeth, vertebrae of the neck, back and tail, the shoulder girdle, both humeri, a first wing phalanx, the pelvis, a shinbone and a calf bone.

facts.statement: In 2003, the fused frontal bones were incorrectly identified as a breast bone.
facts.quote: The fused frontals had in 2003 been incorrectly identified as a breast bone by Wellnhofer.

facts.statement: The fossil is housed in the collection of the Bavarian State Collection for Palaeontology and Historical Geology in Munich.
facts.quote: The fossil is part of the collection of the Bayerische Staatssammlung für Paläontologie und historische Geologie at Munich.

facts.statement: Austriadraco dallavecchiai is a small species with a humerus length of about four centimetres.
facts.quote: Austriadraco dallavecchiai is a small species. Humerus length is about four centimetres.

facts.statement: The shoulder blade is 62% longer than the coracoid.
facts.quote: The shoulder blade is considerably longer, 62%, than the coracoid.

facts.statement: The shinbone is 57.7 millimetres long, reaching 70% of the humerus length and 92% of the first wing finger phalanx length.
facts.quote: The shinbone is relatively long, with a length of 57.7 millimetres attaining 70% of the length of the humerus and 92% of the length of the first phalanx of the (fourth) wingfinger.

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner placed Austriadraco in an undefined family called Austriadraconidae due to uncertain affinities.
facts.quote: Kellner concluded that its affinities were uncertain and placed Austriadraco in a separate, undefined, Austriadraconidae.

facts.statement: Kellner suggested a close relationship with Arcticodactylus based on the shared trait of a short coracoid.
facts.quote: He suggested a close relationship with Arcticodactylus as both taxa shared the trait of a short coracoid.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron grouped Austriadraco with Carniadactylus and Raeticodactylus within the clade Caviramidae.
facts.quote: In 2020, a study upheld by Matthew G. Baron about early pterosaur interrelationships found Austriadraco to group with Carniadactylus, Raeticodactylus, and the Austriadraconidae, which in turn were within a clade called Caviramidae.

facts.statement: Austriadraco is an extinct genus of pterosaur whose remains have been found in the area of present-day Austria.
facts.quote: Austriadraco es un género extinto de pterosaurio que vivió durante el Triásico Superior cuyos restos se han encontrado en el área de la actual Austria.

facts.statement: The only known species, A. dallavecchiai, was previously attributed to Eudimorphodon, and its closest relative may have been Eudimorphodon or Arcticodactylus.
facts.quote: La especie tipo y única conocida —A. dallavecchiai— fue atribuida anteriormente a Eudimorphodon, y su pariente más cercano puede haber sido el propio Eudimorphodon o Arcticodactylus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the specimen represents a juvenile of Eudimorphodon or a distinct genus, with Dalla Vecchia concluding it was neither in 2009.
facts.quote: In 2009, Dalla Vecchia concluded that the specimen was neither a juvenile nor closely related to Eudimorphodon.

rejected.statement: In 2009, Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia concluded that the specimen was neither a juvenile nor closely related to Eudimorphodon.
rejected.quote: In 2009, Dalla Vecchia concluded that the specimen was neither a juvenile nor closely related to Eudimorphodon.
